items.new: I have forgotten to mention that, in many things, Queequeg placed great trust in the excellence of Yojo's judgment and his surprising foresight. He regarded Yojo with considerable esteem, as a fairly decent sort of god who perhaps meant well enough on the whole, but who did not, in all cases, succeed in his well-meaning plans.

items.new: Half hidden in this strange shelter, I finally found someone who looked like he had authority. It was noon, the ship's work was paused, and he was enjoying a break from the burden of command. He sat in an old-fashioned oak chair, wriggling all over with curious carving, its seat formed of a stout interlacing of the same springy material as the wigwam.

items.new: I protested my innocence. I could see that behind the mask of these half-humorous insinuations, this old seaman, as an insulated, Quakerish Nantucketer, was full of his insular prejudices. He was suspicious of all outsiders unless they came from Cape Cod or the Vineyard.

items.new: Such was the person I saw sitting on the stern bench when I followed Captain Peleg down into the cabin. The space between the decks was small. There, bolt upright, sat old Bildad, who always sat that way and never leaned — this to preserve his coat tails. His broad-brimmed hat was placed beside him. His legs were stiffly crossed. His drab clothes were buttoned up to his chin. And with spectacles on his nose, he seemed absorbed in reading from a heavy volume.

items.reason: Source: 'went on spelling away at his book in a mumbling tone'. 'Spelling away' (slowly sounding his way through, which sets up Peleg's thirty-years joke in 16.46) became plain 'reading'.
items.new: "He'll do," said Bildad, looking me over. Then he went on spelling his way through his book in a mumbling tone, quite audible.

items.reason: Source: 'the other and more inconsiderable and scattered owners' lost 'scattered'; 'I did not know but what the stingy old Bildad might have a mighty deal to say' (a possibility) became 'I suspected'; 'Peleg was vainly trying to mend a pen' lost 'vainly'.
items.new: But one thing made me uneasy about getting a generous share of the profits. Ashore, I had heard about both Captain Peleg and his strange old crony Bildad — how, being the principal owners of the Pequod, the other, lesser and scattered owners left nearly all management of the ship's business to these two. And for all I knew, stingy old Bildad might have a great deal of say in hiring the crew, especially since I now found him aboard the Pequod, completely at home in the cabin, reading his Bible as if by his own fireside. While Peleg was vainly trying to sharpen a pen with his jackknife, old Bildad — to my considerable surprise, given that he was such an interested party in these proceedings — paid us no attention at all. He just went on mumbling to himself from his book: "Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth —"

items.reason: Source: 'though he twitched a little as if still nervously agitated'. The 'as if' appearance became fact ('with nervous agitation').
items.new: Alarmed by this terrible outburst between the two principal and responsible owners of the ship, and half thinking of giving up the whole idea of sailing on a vessel so questionably owned and temporarily commanded, I stepped aside from the door to let Bildad escape. Surely he'd want to flee from Peleg's wrath. But to my astonishment, he sat back down on the bench very quietly and showed not the slightest intention of leaving. He seemed completely used to impenitent Peleg and his ways. As for Peleg, after blowing off his rage, he seemed to have no more left in him. He too sat down like a lamb, though he twitched a little, as if still nervously agitated. "Whew!" he finally whistled. "The squall's blown off to leeward, I think. Bildad, you used to be good at sharpening a lance — sharpen that pen for me, will you? My jackknife needs a grindstone. That's it — thank you, Bildad. Now then, young man, Ishmael's your name, didn't you say? Well then, down you go here, Ishmael, for the three hundredth lay."

items.reason: Source: 'in all probability he had been sitting so for upwards of eight or ten hours'. 'upwards of' dropped.
items.new: But no matter what we said, we couldn't drag a single word out of him. I almost felt like pushing him over just to change his position, which was almost unbearable to look at — so painfully and unnaturally stiff. Especially since, in all likelihood, he had been sitting that way for upwards of eight or ten hours, going without his regular meals the whole time.

items.reason: Source: 'he had nothing but his ordinary round jacket on'. A round jacket is a short, tail-less sailor's jacket; 'light jacket' invents a quality the source does not state.
items.new: Giving up on him, I decided to go to bed and sleep. No doubt he would follow before long. But before turning in, I took my heavy bearskin jacket and threw it over him, since it promised to be a very cold night and he had nothing but his ordinary short sailor's jacket on. For some time, no matter what I did, I couldn't fall asleep. I had blown out the candle, and the mere thought of Queequeg — not four feet away — sitting in that miserable position, completely alone in the cold and dark — it made me truly wretched. Think of it: sleeping all night in the same room with a wide-awake pagan squatting in this dreary, inexplicable Ramadan!

items.reason: Source: 'pressed his forehead again against mine' — 'again' (recalling the earlier forehead-pressing of their friendship) dropped.
items.new: But somehow I drifted off at last and knew nothing more until daybreak. Looking over the side of the bed, there squatted Queequeg, as if he had been bolted to the floor. But as soon as the first rays of sun entered the window, up he got, with stiff and creaking joints but a cheerful face. He limped over to where I lay, pressed his forehead against mine again, and said his Ramadan was over.

items.new: "Is that so?" cried Bildad. "Is this Philistine really a member of Deacon Deuteronomy's congregation? I never saw him there, and I pass it every Lord's day."

items.new: "Splice — you mean splice hands," cried Peleg, coming closer. "Young man, you'd better sign on as a missionary instead of a common sailor. I never heard a better sermon. Deacon Deuteronomy — why, Father Mapple himself couldn't beat it, and he's considered something. Come aboard, come aboard — never mind about the papers. I say, tell Quohog there — what do you call him? Tell Quohog to step along. By the great anchor, what a harpoon he's got there! Looks like good stuff, that, and he handles it just right. I say, Quohog, or whatever your name is, have you ever stood in the bow of a whale-boat? Have you ever struck a whale?"

items.new: "And well said — I like hearing a man speak up like that. You're just the right sort for him — exactly the type. Good morning, shipmates, morning! Oh! And when you get there, tell them I've decided not to make one of them."

items.reason: Source: 'I pronounced him in my heart, a humbug' repeats 19.33's 'nothing but a humbug'; the candidate's 'fraud' breaks the deliberate echo that 19.33 keeps.
items.new: I decided to find out for certain whether this ragged Elijah was truly following us. Queequeg and I crossed to the other side of the street and retraced our steps. But Elijah walked straight past without seeming to notice us. This was a relief, and once more — and finally, as it seemed to me — I decided in my heart that he was nothing but a humbug.

items.reason: Source: 'But it seems they always give very long notice in these cases'. 'it seems' and the general 'always' became 'as usual, they gave'.
items.new: The day after Queequeg signed the articles, word was sent to all the inns where the crew was staying that their sea chests had to be on board before nightfall — there was no telling how soon the ship might sail. So Queequeg and I brought our belongings down, though we planned to sleep ashore until the last possible night. But it seems they always give very long notice in these cases, and the ship didn't actually sail for several more days. No surprise there — there was a great deal to be done, and no telling how many details needed attending to before the Pequod was fully equipped.

items.reason: Source: 'nothing should be found wanting in the Pequod, after once fairly getting to sea' (the ship). Immediately after 'if she had anything to say about it' (Aunt Charity), 'once she was properly at sea' reads as if Charity were going to sea.
items.new: Chief among those doing this ferrying was Captain Bildad's sister, a thin old lady of fierce and tireless determination, but genuinely kindhearted. She seemed resolved that, if she had anything to say about it, nothing would be found lacking on the Pequod once the ship was fairly at sea. One time she came aboard with a jar of pickles for the steward's pantry. Another time with a bunch of quill pens for the chief mate's desk, where he kept his log. Another with a roll of flannel for the small of someone's rheumatic back. No woman ever better deserved her name, which was Charity — Aunt Charity, as everyone called her. And like a sister of charity, this charitable Aunt Charity bustled here and there, ready to turn her hand and heart to anything that promised safety, comfort, or consolation to everyone aboard a ship in which her beloved brother Bildad had an interest, and in which she herself owned a score or two of well-saved dollars.

items.new: "Stop!" cried a voice. Its owner came up close behind us, laid a hand on both our shoulders, and then slipped himself in between us. Stooping forward slightly in the uncertain twilight, he peered strangely from Queequeg to me. It was Elijah.

items.new: "No, no, no — I wasn't aware of that," said Elijah, slowly and wonderingly looking from me to Queequeg and back with the strangest glances.

items.reason: Source: 'just as if they were to be joint-commanders at sea, as well as to all appearances in port' ('to all appearances' dropped); 'steering her well out to sea' lost 'well'; 'before they quit the ship for good with the pilot' lost 'for good'.
items.new: How about that! Here at the very moment of departure, Captain Peleg and Captain Bildad were running the show on the quarter-deck, just as if they were going to be the joint commanders at sea as well as, to all appearances, in port. As for Captain Ahab, there was still no sign of him. They said he was in the cabin. But the idea was that his presence wasn't at all necessary for getting the ship underway and steering her well out to sea. That was really the pilot's job, and since he hadn't fully recovered — so they said — Captain Ahab stayed below. All of this seemed natural enough. In the merchant service, many captains never show themselves on deck for some time after the anchor is raised, but stay at the cabin table having a farewell party with their shore friends before those friends leave the ship for good with the pilot.

items.reason: Source: 'Captain Peleg in the act of withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity'. 'boot' replaces 'leg', which 22.10 picks up ('using his leg very freely').
items.new: Meanwhile, overseeing the other end of the ship, Captain Peleg raged and swore astern in the most frightful manner. I almost thought he'd sink the ship before the anchor could be raised. I involuntarily paused at my handspike and told Queequeg to do the same, thinking of the dangers we faced in starting a voyage with such a devil for a pilot. I was comforting myself with the thought that pious Bildad might offer some salvation, despite his seven hundred and seventy-seventh lay, when I felt a sudden sharp jab in my rear. Turning around, I was horrified to see Captain Peleg withdrawing his leg from my immediate vicinity. That was my first kick.

items.new: Never did those sweet words sound more beautiful to me than at that moment. They were full of hope and fulfillment. Despite this frigid winter night on the wild Atlantic, despite my wet feet and even wetter jacket, it seemed to me there were still many pleasant harbors ahead — meadows and glades so eternally springlike that the grass that shot up in the spring remains, untrodden and unwilted, at midsummer.
